name: Zugzwang
goal: You can win a position where the opponent would be fine if they could pass, by making the move that leaves them only bad moves.

intro.text: In some positions the side to move would gladly pass, because every possible move makes things worse, but passing is not allowed. That is zugzwang, from a German word meaning roughly "forced to move". It comes up most in endgames with only kings and pawns, where a king guards something important and every step it takes gives that up. You win these positions with a move that hands the turn to your opponent, often by taking the opposition or with a waiting move.

parts.title: One king, two pawns
parts.keyIdea: Taking the opposition can leave the other king with no good square: wherever it steps, it gives something up.
parts.text: From a game played on Lichess. You are Black. White's king on f4 guards the f5 pawn, and from g4 it could guard both f5 and h5. If it ever has to step away from them, a pawn falls.

credit.authors: Lichess; the position is from a game played there

notes.text: Your king faces White's king with one square between them, f6 against f4. Both white pawns are now blocked, so White has to move the king, and only one square, g4, still guards both pawns.
Your king attacks the f5 pawn from the other side. White has to move again: no square the king can reach still guards f5, and 54.f6 just gives the pawn away.
The pawn falls, and your king is close to the h5 pawn as well. With two pawns against one and the more active king, you are winning.

parts.title: Running out of moves
parts.keyIdea: When you want the other side to be the one who moves, a waiting move with a pawn hands them the turn.
parts.text: From a game played on Lichess. You are White. Your king would love to get to c5 or d5, but Black's king on d6 guards both squares. Count the waiting moves each side has left with its pawns.

credit.authors: Lichess; the position is from a game played there

notes.text: A waiting move: your king stays put and Black must move. Black's a- and g-pawns are blocked and 35...c5 just loses a pawn, so Black's king has to step back. 35.a3 would not work, because Black answers with the waiting move 35...a4, and it is White who runs out of useful moves.
Black's king stepped back, so yours walks in. On c5 it attacks the c6 pawn and is heading for b6 and the a5 pawn.
Black's king came back to guard c6, so your king goes after a5 instead. Black cannot defend both pawns, and you win one of them, with a won endgame.

parts.title: Zugzwang that mates
parts.keyIdea: Take away the last free squares, and the opponent may be forced to play a move that loses at once.
parts.text: From a game played on Lichess. You are Black. White's king on a4 is hemmed in by your pawns on a6 and b6. Look at which moves White would still have after your next move.

credit.authors: Lichess; the position is from a game played there

notes.text: Your king covers b3, and your pawns already cover a5 and b5, so White's king cannot move at all. The a-pawn is stuck behind its own king, which leaves White only one legal move: pushing the b-pawn to b5.
The pawn takes on b5 with check, and White's king has nowhere to go. It is mate, and it only happened because White had to move.
